question: You examine a 30-year-old man brought by police after an alleged assault. You find three contusions on the back of the forearms (dorsal surface), one contusion on the palm, and no injuries on the face or anterior trunk. Based on this wound distribution, what is the most appropriate medicolegal inference?

answers.text: The wound distribution is consistent with defence wounds, suggesting the victim was conscious and attempting to protect himself at the time of the assault.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Defence wounds are injuries sustained on the parts of the body used instinctively to deflect blows — classically the dorsal forearms (blocking overhead strikes), the palms (warding off frontal strikes), and the outer aspects of the hands. Their presence supports that the victim was conscious and reactive during the assault, which is important both medically and legally.

answers.text: The wound distribution is consistent with self-inflicted injuries, because the contusions are confined to the upper limbs and have a uniform pattern.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Self-inflicted injuries are more commonly on accessible body surfaces, typically in accessible areas on the same side as the dominant hand, and often on the anterior trunk or inner forearm. Dorsal forearm + palmar contusions from an 'assault' context strongly suggest defence injuries, not self-infliction.

answers.text: No medicolegal inference can be drawn; wound distribution alone is insufficient without a weapon recovered.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Wound distribution is itself a forensic finding from which meaningful inferences can be drawn. The medicolegal examination and opinion does not require a weapon to be recovered before a report can be written. The pattern here supports defence wounds and should be documented as such.

answers.text: The wound distribution suggests the injuries were inflicted from behind while the victim was facing away, consistent with a pre-planned ambush.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Dorsal forearm contusions indicate the victim raised his arms to shield himself — this is a defensive action facing the assailant, not evidence of being struck from behind. An ambush-from-behind pattern would more typically show injuries to the posterior trunk, head, and posterior upper arms without defensive forearm wounds.

overallFeedback.feedback: Defence wounds classically occur on the dorsal forearms (blocking overhead or lateral blows) and palms (blocking frontal strikes). This distribution is a strong indicator of a conscious, reactive victim — a significant medicolegal finding to include in the MLC.

Correct. Defence wounds are a key interpretive skill: dorsal forearms + palms = classic blocking pattern = victim was conscious and reactive. Always note defence wounds explicitly in your MLC opinion.
